name: Turkish Psychedelic
about: Turkish psychedelia is the Western crate-digger's name for the stranger end of Anadolu rock: the records from roughly 1968 to 1980 where fuzz, wah-wah, Farfisa and primitive synthesizers met the bağlama, the zurna and the asymmetrical rhythms of Anatolian folk. Erkin Koray's Elektronik Türküler is the keystone, Mustafa Özkent's instrumental funk and Zafer Dilek's oyun havaları the dancefloor end, Selda Bağcan's fuzz-laden protest songs the emotional one. Most of it was released on 45s and only compiled decades later by labels such as Finders Keepers, Pharaway Sounds and Uzelli, which is how it reached DJs and samplers abroad. A revival led by BaBa ZuLa, Altın Gün and Derya Yıldırım & Grup Şimşek has made it a living style again.

albums.title: Elektronik Türküler
albums.why: Koray's masterpiece, electric bağlama and tape echo on folk tunes stretched to fifteen minutes; the keystone of Turkish psychedelia and its most sampled record.

albums.title: Gençlik İle Elele
albums.why: Özkent's instrumental funk arrangements of folk melodies, with Moog, clavinet and crisp breakbeats; a Finders Keepers rediscovery that became a DJ staple.

albums.title: Selda
albums.why: Fuzz guitar, saz and a cutting voice on songs about poverty and prison; the heaviest and most sampled of Selda's 1970s records.
A science-fiction concept album with Kurtalan Ekspres, Moog and saz across prog suites; Manço at his most ambitious and strangest.

albums.title: Erkin Koray
albums.why: The singles compiled on Koray's first LP are the root of the whole style: fuzz guitar bent to microtonal scales, and a voice from the Istanbul street.

albums.title: Anadolu Pop
albums.why: Moğollar's mostly instrumental manifesto, cut in Paris and award-winning, with folk themes over a rock rhythm section and an early taste of synthesizer.

albums.title: Nem Kaldı
albums.why: Karaca and Dervişan's heavy, organ-driven political folk rock, the most forceful band sound of the mid-1970s scene.

albums.title: Hürel Arşiv
albums.why: Three brothers with a three-necked guitar and a taste for odd metres; the heaviest and most prog-minded of the classic singles bands.

albums.title: Nedir Ne Değildir?
albums.why: Akbayram's Alevi protest songs given fuzz and organ by Dostlar; a record whose politics and grooves are equally fierce.

albums.title: Oyun Havaları
albums.why: Dilek's electrified dance tunes with drum machine and fuzz saz, instrumental and relentless; the record DJs reach for first.

albums.title: Dünden Bugüne
albums.why: Manço's early singles collected, including 'Dağlar Dağlar', the biggest Turkish hit of its era; where Anatolian psychedelia found its pop voice.

albums.title: Parka
albums.why: Karaca's sharpest record with Dervişan, longer suites and harder rock under the leftist lyrics that would soon send him into exile.

albums.title: Not Defterimden
albums.why: Kızılok's quiet acoustic record is the gentlest thing here, folk rock with a melancholy that psychedelic listeners have adopted anyway.

albums.title: Love, Peace & Poetry: Turkish Psychedelic Music
albums.why: The QDK Media volume that first put the Turkish scene on the international map; a well-chosen primer of 1960s and 1970s singles.

albums.title: Turkish Freakout: Psych-Folk Singles 1969-80
albums.why: Bouzouki Joe's compilation of psych-folk 45s, fuzzier and funkier than the earlier surveys; the second essential primer.

albums.title: Türküz Türkü Çağırırız
albums.why: Mazhar and Fuat's harmony-folk album is a softer, more acoustic cousin of the fuzz records, with light psychedelic touches.

albums.title: Psychebelly Dance Music
albums.why: BaBa ZuLa's dub-and-saz psychedelia that announced a new Istanbul underground; loose, long and hypnotic.

albums.title: On
albums.why: The Amsterdam band's debut of Koray and Manço covers over disco bass and synths; the record that started the revival.

albums.title: Gece
albums.why: The Grammy-nominated follow-up, tighter and more electronic; the revival's commercial peak.

albums.title: Hologram İmparatorluğu
albums.why: Akyol's second record, surf guitar and Anatolian scales under a voice modelled on Selda; the most original of the new Istanbul wave.

albums.title: Kar Yağar
albums.why: Yıldırım's bağlama and voice with a Franco-German band on a record of real groove and care for the old songs.

albums.title: Mantra Moderne
albums.why: Kit Sebastian's Anglo-Turkish duo mixing Anatolian scales with French pop and tropicália; a stylish Mr Bongo record.

albums.title: Anadolu Ejderi
albums.why: Akyol's fourth, more varied and theatrical, with the Anatolian dragon of the title standing for a country's contradictions.

albums.title: DOST 1
albums.why: Yıldırım and Grup Şimşek's third record, originals alongside folk songs, warmer and jazzier than Kar Yağar.

note: Most of the classic era came out on singles, so several entries are first-LP collections or later compilations rather than studio albums.
